t: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree III: Intersection of Parent Chains
o: Unlike the classic LCA task, we receive no root — only two nodes whose parent pointers chain upward. Each chain is effectively a linked list ending at the root, so the LCA is exactly where the two lists intersect: in Example 1 the chains 5 -> 3 -> ... and 1 -> 3 -> ... first coincide at 3. Example 2 highlights the self-ancestor rule: q = 4 lies beneath p = 5, so the intersection is p itself. With up to 10^5 nodes, the answer should come from climbing O(height) parent links rather than searching the whole tree.
k: No root given? Treat parent pointers as two linked lists meeting at the root — the LCA is their intersection node.
Hashing the ancestors of p and climbing from q finds the first shared node in linear time.
The two-pointer switch trick (jumping to the OTHER start node upon falling off the top) equalizes depth differences and finds the meeting point in O(1) space.

a.i: Record every ancestor of p, including p itself, in a hash set. Then walk from q toward the root; the first node already present in the set is the lowest common ancestor, since any lower shared ancestor would have been encountered sooner, and the common root guarantees termination.
s: Climb from p to the root, inserting each visited node into a set.
Climb from q upward until reaching a node contained in the set.
a.t: O(dp + dq) — two parent-chain climbs, where dp and dq are the depths of p and q.

a.i: Mirror the elegant linked-list-intersection solution. Pointer a starts at p and b at q; whichever pointer falls off the root teleports to the OTHER starting node. Each pointer then travels exactly dp + dq steps before they meet precisely at the LCA — the teleport cancels out the depth difference. Constant extra space and no allocations.
s: Initialize a = p and b = q.
While a != b: advance a to a.parent, or to q if it fell off the top; advance b to b.parent, or to p if it fell off.
Return a once the pointers coincide.
a.t: O(dp + dq) — each pointer traverses at most both chains before meeting.
a.sp: O(1) — two references and nothing else.

w: Show the set version first for clarity, then offer pointer switching as the O(1)-space refinement — interviewers love the connection to Linked List Cycle II-style intersection problems. Termination relies on p and q living in the SAME tree (guaranteed here); in a forest they would never meet, so production code adds a step bound or null check. Do not "reset to the root" — the root is not provided, which is the whole twist of this variant. Follow-ups: LCA of k nodes (fold pairwise or intersect ancestor sets), distance between p and q via depth sums minus twice the LCA depth, or supporting parent updates.
